Ear Reverence

Sound for Music

seventy-nine pieces · 4 hours 57 minutes 2 seconds

Each line is drawn from the loudness of its piece. Press anywhere on a line to play from there.

001

Tel Ories

3:35

It opens with a small rising figure, then a rush of noise. After that, short bright notes fall in clusters over a low rumble, and the clusters crowd closer toward the end.

A few small tones climb in the quiet, and at eight seconds a rush of noise wipes them away. Then the notes begin. They come in twos and threes over a low rumble, struck and left to ring, with gaps between the groups. It is a kind of rain with rules. Around the halfway mark a band of held tones sits underneath for half a minute and goes. After that the groups arrive sooner and reach higher. The last half minute is crowded with them.

0:00
002

Ded Calas

9:49

Nearly ten minutes. The first four are sparse, with separate sounds and sharp jolts. Then it thickens into a broad, loud mass of stacked tones, like an orchestra, and ends on low held chords.

It fades in, and for a minute and a half the sounds stay separate. From 1:25 sharp jolts cut in, most of them three seconds apart, and they keep coming for nearly three minutes. At 4:20 everything thickens at once, tone stacked on tone. If it is an orchestra, it is sitting a little to your left. Several times it cuts out and comes back, and the longest gap, at 7:26, lasts eighteen seconds. At 8:52 the low chords come in. They are still at full strength when the piece stops.

0:00
003

Omet Arg

12:36

Twelve and a half minutes at one steady level. A high, winding line keeps moving over a fast, fine patter, and early on a low swell passes underneath.

Twelve and a half minutes, and no minute is noticeably louder than another. The line on top wanders over two octaves, and most of its notes are gone in half a second. It is closer to handwriting than to a tune. What changes is underneath. A low part runs for four and a half minutes, with one deep swell from 1:45 to 2:30. Then it drops out, and for nearly three minutes the line has very little under it. At 7:20 a single low note comes in and holds to the end.

0:00

The roar comes up from nothing and thickens for forty-seven seconds. It takes that long to build and less than a second to leave. What is left is clear notes, held and overlapping, under a thin high shimmer. Lower down, about every six seconds, a soft note knocks twice. The knocking had already begun under the roar.

From there the piece is louder, and a slow swell rises and falls through it about every ten seconds.

It begins with separate, spaced notes and fills in steadily, getting louder the whole way. By the end, sliding calls rise and fall over a held tone.

Spaced notes at first, with quiet between them, then more and more until the gaps are gone, and louder all the way. Its bass is a visitor. A low note walks in at a minute and a half, beats twice a second for a little over a minute, and walks out. The piece goes on growing without it.

A tone is struck and left to die away, over and over, with a soft haze above it each time. The first strikes are missing something, and you only learn what at 0:46, when one lands with a floor under it that the others never had.

Ance Nal

A plain tone switches on and off over a low bed for a minute and a half. A few hard knocks break in, and then it is hushed. The low bed is no bed. It is the struck tone of the piece before this one, the same strike, landing twice as often.

The loudest piece of the seventy-nine, and one of the shortest: a thick chord at full strength that keeps dipping for a moment and coming straight back. Nobody could sing along. Nine tenths of it lies below the lowest note a bass can reach.

It starts from almost nothing and builds, layer on layer, into something like an orchestra holding a chord. There are two As in it, nearly a quarter-tone apart. The left ear gets only the higher one. The right ear gets both, and has to live with it.

One soft chord of pure held tones, four minutes of it, with a note here and there growing brighter and dimmer. Nothing is struck. Turn the treble all the way down and listen again. You will not hear the difference: there is nothing up there to take away.

Close to two minutes of voices, many at once, busy from the first second to the last. You would expect a crowd to be the unruly one. Of the seventy-nine pieces, this is the one whose level moves least: it never once dips, not for a tenth of a second.

Quick mid tones, layered close, and for forty-four seconds they lean on a pulse, one push every two seconds. Then a second of almost nothing. It comes back fuller, with a low part under it, and without the pulse. Nobody is counting any more.

A chord that keeps adding notes, and short bright bursts that keep cutting across it: one every five seconds or so in the first minute, and closer together after that. It does them no good. The chord takes every one and goes on growing, and it ends close to the loudest it has been.

A low, slow piece: a deep tone settles in after the first minute, and soft mid tones come and go above it. The lowest note of all is slower still. It starts on a D sharp, and by the end, three and a half minutes later, it has climbed two keys, to F, with a minute off on the way.

One deep note that never moves, and over it plain tones, switched on and off. Then a rougher sound breaks in, with bursts of noise. The interruption gets as long as the opening got, a minute and a half. When the tones have the floor again they are given half that, and the piece is over.

A deep thump runs the whole way, under mid tones that rise and fall in slow arcs. Each thump is two: a strong beat, a weaker one close behind, then a wait. A heart goes like that, and this one goes at thirty-eight to the minute, about half the speed of yours. Whatever it belongs to is very calm or very large.

A ticking, shimmering ground, a very high tone ringing over it, and one line that wanders: up from an A, and back down. It is the last of the seventy-nine, and it does not wind down. In its final seconds the line comes back to the A it started on, just in time, and the sound stops.
